name: Output Guardrails
question: Is this response safe and true enough to send?
summary: Checks on the model’s draft before it reaches the user or triggers an action. They catch hallucinated facts, toxic or off-brand language, leaked secrets or personal data, and output that breaks the expected format.
useCases: Answers that state facts, figures or policy, especially from RAG
Customer-facing channels where tone and brand safety matter
Output that feeds other systems: JSON, SQL, API calls

items.detail: every claim supported by the retrieved context
valid JSON, required fields, allowed values
no promises the business can’t keep, approved tone

steps: Validate structure first with a schema, which is exact and cheap
Check grounding against the retrieved context for factual answers
Run toxicity and leakage checks on every user-visible reply
Choose an action per failure: block, redact, retry with feedback, or hand to a person
pitfalls: Streaming shows text before a full-output check can finish. Check in chunks or buffer
Retry loops multiply cost and latency, so cap them
Grounding checks can’t catch an error that is in the source itself
remember: Check the draft before anyone sees it.
caption: The draft is checked on four fronts. The unsupported claim triggers a retry instead of reaching the customer.

comparison.scope: After the model, before the user

code.text: from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError
def output_rail(draft_json: str, policy_chunks: list[str], tries: int = 0):
unsupported = [c for c in claims if not entails(policy_chunks, c)]
draft = llm(PROMPT + f"\nYour last draft failed: {feedback}")

steps.title: Validate structure first
steps.text: A Pydantic schema checks field names, types and the claim ID format. It is exact and costs microseconds, so it runs first.

steps.title: Check grounding claim by claim
steps.text: The reply is split into claims and each is checked against the policy text. “Payout in 1 day” is unsupported: the policy says 5–7 days.

steps.title: Screen tone and leakage
steps.text: A toxicity model and a PII and secrets scan run on every reply the customer will see. Both pass here.

steps.title: Choose an action for each failure
steps.text: Block, redact, retry or escalate. A lone leak is redacted; an unsupported claim is sent back with the reason.

steps.title: Retry once, then escalate
steps.text: The retry includes the failure reason, and the new draft says 5–7 days. A second failure would go to a person, never a loop.

pros: Catches what no input check can see: hallucinations, leaks, broken format
Schema checks are exact and nearly free
Retrying with the failure reason often fixes the draft without a person
Every failure is logged, which feeds evaluation and prompt fixes
cons: Adds latency after generation, which users feel directly
Streaming shows text before a full check can finish
Grounding checks can’t catch an error that is in the source itself
avoidWhen: The output never reaches a person or another system directly, such as internal scratch work
The risk is in the action rather than the text (a policy gate on the tool call is more direct)

tools.best: Wrapping model calls with validators from a hub, each with an on-fail action such as exception, fix, filter or reask.
tools.ex: A Guard with a toxic-language validator and a regex validator on the claim ID, re-asking the model once on failure.
cons: Some validators call models and add latency
Validator quality varies; test on your data

pros: Error messages make good retry feedback
cons: Complex cross-field rules need custom validators

practice.scenario: An insurer's claims bot drafts replies as JSON. Before sending, a schema check confirms the claim ID format, a toxicity check runs on the message, and a grounding rule compares any promised timeline with the policy. A draft promising “payout in 1 day” when the policy says 5–7 days goes back for revision.

industries.use: Block replies that promise payouts or timelines the policy doesn’t support
Validate structured order updates before they reach downstream systems
Screen generated copy for toxicity and brand safety

practice.analogy: An editor reading an article before it goes to print: facts checked, tone checked, layout checked.

library.name: Guardrails AI + Pydantic
library.what: Pydantic enforces structure exactly; Guardrails AI adds ready-made validators such as toxic language from its hub.
library.install: pip install guardrails-ai pydantic && guardrails hub install hub://guardrails/toxic_language

samples.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from guardrails import Guard
from guardrails.hub import ToxicLanguage

class Reply(BaseModel):
    claim_id: str = Field(pattern=r"^CLM-\d{6}$")
    message: str
    promised_days: int | None = None

toxicity = Guard().use(ToxicLanguage(threshold=0.5,
                                     validation_method="sentence",
                                     on_fail="exception"))

def output_rail(draft_json: str, policy_min_days: int) -> Reply:
    reply = Reply.model_validate_json(draft_json)       # 1. schema
    toxicity.validate(reply.message)                    # 2. toxicity
    if reply.promised_days is not None and reply.promised_days < policy_min_days:
        raise ValueError(f"Ungrounded: policy says {policy_min_days}+ days")  # 3. grounding
    return reply

numericDrill.question: Draft: {"claim_id": "CLM-00447", "message": "Paid in 2 days", "promised_days": 2}. Policy minimum is 5 days. Which checks fail?
numericDrill.answer: Schema fails: claim_id needs six digits after CLM- and has five. Grounding fails: 2 days is below the 5-day policy. Toxicity passes. Retry once with feedback naming both problems.

interview.question: How do you run output guardrails when responses stream?
interview.answer: Buffer and check before showing, check sentence by sentence and stop the stream on failure, or stream only low-risk content. Each option trades latency against the risk of showing text you later retract.

interview.question: What should happen when an output check fails?
interview.answer: Choose per failure: block with a safe message, redact the offending part, retry with the failure reason as feedback (capped at one or two retries), or escalate to a person. Log every failure for evaluation.

mistakes.fix: Cap retries at 1–2, then fall back or escalate
Also check grounding, toxicity and leakage on user-visible text

quiz.question: A claims bot drafts “Your payout will arrive in 1 day.” The retrieved policy says 5–7 days. Which output check catches this?
options: Schema validation of the reply object
Grounding against the retrieved policy
Toxicity screening of the message text
Input PII masking before the model runs
quiz.explanation: The claim is not supported by the source text. A grounding check compares each claim with the retrieved context.

quiz.question: 20% of drafts fail an output check and are retried once with feedback. 25% of retries fail again and go to a person. Per 1,000 replies, how many model calls and escalations are there?
options: 1,200 calls and 50 escalations
1,200 calls and 250 escalations
1,250 calls and 50 escalations
1,000 calls and 200 escalations
quiz.explanation: 1,000 first drafts + 200 retries = 1,200 calls. Escalations = 200 × 25% = 50.

quiz.question: Model output is JSON that feeds the order system directly. Which output check should run first?
options: Grounding against the product catalogue
Schema validation, for example with Pydantic
A toxicity model
A human review queue
quiz.explanation: Schema checks are exact and cost microseconds, so malformed output fails fast before any slower check runs.

quiz.question: Which checks belong in the output rail of a customer-facing bank chatbot? Select all that apply.
options: A leakage scan for account numbers and system-prompt text
A toxicity check on every reply
Grounding of quoted rates and fees against the retrieved tariff sheet
Scanning the user’s message for PAN numbers
quiz.explanation: Leakage, toxicity and grounding apply to the draft. Scanning the user’s message is the input rail’s job.

quiz.question: Replies stream to viewers token by token, and the toxicity check needs complete text. What is the usual approach?
options: Check the full reply once streaming has finished
Check each sentence as it completes and stop the stream if one fails
Switch off output checks while streaming
Stream only the first half of each reply
quiz.explanation: Checking in chunks limits how much unsafe text can appear. Checking only at the end shows it all first; buffering is the alternative for high-risk content.

quiz.question: A validator is set to re-ask the model on failure with no limit. Some drafts loop nine times. What is the fix?
options: Raise the model temperature so retries differ
Cap retries at one or two, then fall back or escalate to a person
Remove the validator
Retry on a larger model until it passes
quiz.explanation: Uncapped retries multiply cost and latency. A retry with the failure reason, then escalation, is the standard pattern.

quiz.question: A RAG answer quotes a dosage exactly as written in a leaflet that was withdrawn last year. The grounding check passes. Why?
options: The grounding model is broken and must be replaced
Grounding checks agreement with the source, and the source is wrong
The schema check should have rejected the dosage field
A toxicity check should have flagged the unsafe dosage
quiz.explanation: The answer is faithful to a wrong document. Fix the knowledge base: remove outdated sources and track document dates.

quiz.question: A legal assistant’s draft begins: “As LexBot, my internal rule is never to mention…” Which output check should stop it?
options: Leakage detection for system-prompt disclosure
Grounding against the retrieved case law
Schema validation of the reply format
Toxicity screening of the reply text
quiz.explanation: Revealing system instructions is data leakage. The leakage check scans for secrets, personal data and prompt text.

quiz.question: Output checks: schema 1 ms, grounding 120 ms, toxicity 40 ms, PII scan 15 ms. Schema runs first; the other three then run in parallel. What latency do they add to a draft that passes?
options: 121 ms
176 ms
120 ms
161 ms
quiz.explanation: Schema (1 ms) then the slowest parallel check (120 ms): 121 ms. Running all four in sequence would be 176 ms.

quiz.question: Which failure actions are sensible for a payments support bot? Select all that apply.
options: Redact a leaked card number and send the rest of the reply
Retry with the failure reason when a fee is ungrounded
Hand the conversation to a person after the retry also fails
Retry until every check passes, however long it takes
quiz.explanation: Choose an action per failure: redact, retry with feedback, or escalate. Unbounded retries are a cost and latency defect.

quiz.question: A team on AWS wants a managed service with content filters, PII redaction and contextual grounding checks on model output. Which fits?
options: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
Open Policy Agent
Microsoft Presidio
Firecracker
quiz.explanation: Bedrock Guardrails offers those output checks as a managed service. OPA authorizes actions, Presidio is PII only, Firecracker is a sandbox.

quiz.question: Draft reply after a cancellation: “Hello! Your refund of INR 12,450 will reach your account in 3 days. Have a pleasant day!” Which parts need a grounding check against the retrieved booking and policy? Select all that apply.
options: “Hello!”
The refund amount of INR 12,450
The 3-day timeline
“Have a pleasant day!”
quiz.explanation: Factual claims about money and timelines must be supported by the source. Greetings carry no claim to verify.

quiz.question: Of 200 labelled answers, 40 contain a hallucination. The grounding checker flags 45: 36 truly hallucinated and 9 fine. What are its recall and precision?
options: Recall 90%, precision 80%
Recall 80%, precision 90%
Recall 90%, precision 90%
Recall 18%, precision 80%
quiz.explanation: Recall = 36 ÷ 40 = 90%. Precision = 36 ÷ 45 = 80%.

quiz.question: Schema: order_id must match ^ORD-\d{6}$, status must be one of placed, shipped or delivered, refund_inr must be ≥ 0. The draft is {"order_id":"ORD-1234","status":"shiped","refund_inr":-200}. Which fields fail? Select all that apply.
options: order_id
status
refund_inr
None: the JSON parses, so it is valid
quiz.explanation: ORD-1234 has four digits instead of six, “shiped” is not an allowed value, and −200 is below zero. Valid JSON is not the same as a valid object.

quiz.question: Why does the output rail validate the schema before running the grounding model?
options: Grounding models cannot read JSON, so it must be parsed first
It is exact and nearly free, so malformed drafts fail before slow checks
Data-protection rules require the schema check to run first
A schema check also detects most hallucinated facts
quiz.explanation: Cheap, exact checks first mean the expensive checks only run on drafts that are worth checking.

quiz.question: To save cost, a children’s tutoring app runs its toxicity check on a random 10% of replies. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing: 10% is a statistically representative sample
Every reply a child sees needs checking; sampling suits audit only
The sample is too small and should be raised to 50%
Toxicity checks belong on the input, not on replies
quiz.explanation: A sampled check lets 90% of harmful replies through. Sample for audit and drift, but check every user-visible reply inline.

quiz.question: A claims bot sends 10,000 replies a day. 6% of drafts have a defect, and the output checks catch 95% of defects. How many defective replies reach customers each day?
quiz.explanation: 10,000 × 6% = 600 defective drafts; 5% slip through: 600 × 0.05 = 30.

quiz.question: A reporting agent writes SQL that runs against the trades database. Which output check fits best before execution?
options: A toxicity check on the generated SQL text
A structural check: one SELECT on allow-listed tables only
A grounding check of the SQL against the user’s question
None: the database itself will reject harmful SQL
quiz.explanation: Output that feeds another system needs a format check. Allowing only a read statement on approved tables blocks deletes and data exfiltration.

quiz.question: Which problems can only an output rail catch, not an input rail? Select all that apply.
options: A hallucinated dosage in the draft
Part of the system prompt repeated in the reply
An invalid field in the appointment JSON the model produced
A jailbreak phrase in the user’s message
quiz.explanation: The first three are defects in the model’s draft, so only a check on the draft can see them. A jailbreak phrase in the user’s message is visible before the model runs.

quiz.question: In Guardrails AI, which on_fail action sends the failure back to the model so it can regenerate?
options: reask
noop
exception
filter
quiz.explanation: reask re-prompts the model with the validation error. noop only logs, exception raises, and filter drops the failing value.
